Wrong: "My monitor is 165 Hz, so the console will get 120 Hz."Right: Microsoft: some monitors support 120 Hz over DisplayPort but not over HDMI, and Xbox outputs HDMI. Check the HDMI input limits. Source: Xbox Support, checked 2026-10-18. Wrong: "Any USB-C charger or the old Switch adapter works on the Switch 2 dock."Right: Nintendo: HAC-002 cannot power the dock. Wrong: "A cheap DisplayPort-to-HDMI adapter is fine for the Steam Deck dock."Right: Valve: passive DP-to-HDMI adapters are not supported. Use an active adapter. Source: Steam Support, checked 2026-10-18. Wrong: "If the box says HDMI 2.1, the cable is fine."Right: HDMI Licensing Administrator: look for the Ultra High Speed HDMI Cable Certification Label (scannable QR) and the cable name on the jacket. Updated: 2026-10-18 · Sources checked: 2026-10-18 Short answer: connect the console directly to the screen's HDMI input first and remove receivers, splitters and adapters. If the screen stays black, use the maker's low-resolution recovery (table below) instead of resetting the console. For 120 Hz, the screen must accept 120 Hz over HDMI; a monitor's DisplayPort refresh rate does not count for an HDMI path. Confidence: OEM support pages (Sony, Microsoft, Nintendo, Valve, ASUS, Lenovo) + HDMI Licensing Administrator • checked 2026-10-18 • UNKNOWN where no OEM statement Find your fix Device PlayStation 5 Xbox Series X Xbox Series S Nintendo Switch 2 (docked) Steam Deck ROG Xbox Ally X (2025) ROG Xbox Ally (2025) Lenovo Legion Go (PSREF 8AHP2 / 8ASP2) Symptom No signal / black screen 120 Hz missing or greyed out Wrong or low resolution / 4K not offered Works direct, fails through receiver, splitter, dock or adapter Flicker, dropouts or picture cuts out ROG Xbox Ally (2025) · 120 Hz missing or greyed out UNKNOWNVideo out: 2x USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C with DisplayPort and power delivery (DisplayPort version not stated). Stated modes: UNKNOWN.UNKNOWN DisplayPort version and maximum external refresh rate: UNKNOWN (not stated on the ASUS spec page).Deep guide: usb c hub vs dock Get the picture back: official recovery per device These are the makers' own routes to force a picture a screen will accept. They change display settings only; none of them is a factory reset. DeviceOfficial recoverySource (checked 2026-10-18) Xbox Series XEject any disc. Hold Power 10 s to turn off. Hold Power + Eject until the second beep (about 10 s). Starts at 640 × 480; then choose a resolution in TV & display options.Xbox Support: blank TV screen Xbox Series SNo Eject button: hold the Xbox button + Pair button until the second beep. Same 640 × 480 start.Xbox Support: blank TV screen PlayStation 5Hold power 3 s to turn off. Hold power until the second beep (about 7 s later). Connect the controller by USB, press PS. Option 2: Change Video Output → Change Resolution or Change HDCP Mode. Other Safe Mode options can delete data.PlayStation: Safe Mode Steam DeckUnplug from the dock. Display menu → External display safe mode On. Plug back in; the Deck picks a low resolution and refresh rate.Steam Support: Docking the Steam Deck Nintendo Switch 2UNKNOWN: no low-resolution mode in the Nintendo page we opened. Nintendo's order: NGN-01 adapter (or ≥54W) on the dock, Ultra High Speed HDMI, console powers and charges undocked, reset adapter 20 s, console screen goes black when docked, remove splitters, TV VRR off.Nintendo Support: no video output in TV mode ROG Xbox Ally / Ally X, Legion GoUNKNOWN: no OEM external-display recovery page found for these handhelds. Use a port the maker lists with DisplayPort (table below) and the USB-C checks in our hub-vs-dock guide.ASUS spec · Lenovo PSREF 120 Hz and resolution: what each maker actually states DeviceVideo outStated modes / ruleSource PlayStation 5HDMI (HDMI 2.1 specification)4K 120 Hz needs a screen that claims it, current screen firmware, the screen's HDMI 2.1 port, the supplied or an Ultra High Speed cable, Resolution Automatic/2160p and Video Transfer Rate Automatic. Test 1440p Output checks 60/120 Hz and VRR at 1440p.PlayStation Xbox Series XHDMIMicrosoft's articles disagree. Set up 4K gaming at 120 Hz: 4K at 120 fps with an Xbox Series X, an Ultra High Speed HDMI cable that supports HDMI 2.1 and an HDMI 2.1 TV; without HDMI 2.1, 120 Hz at a lower resolution. How to change the TV display settings: "120Hz is only available for 1080p and 1440p". Whether 4K 120 Hz works on your setup: UNKNOWN until the console offers it. Both: the display must support 120 Hz over HDMI.Xbox 4K 120 · Xbox display settings Xbox Series SHDMISet up 4K gaming at 120 Hz: 120 Hz at a lower resolution, and "If you own an Xbox Series S and wish to game in 4K@120Hz, you’ll need to acquire a certified Ultra High Speed HDMI cable." How to change the TV display settings: "120Hz is only available for 1080p and 1440p". 4K 120 Hz on Series S: UNKNOWN.Xbox 4K 120 · Xbox display settings Nintendo Switch 2Dock HDMI (TV mode)Up to 3840×2160 at 60 fps; 120 fps when 1920×1080 or 2560×1440 is selected; HDR10; VRR up to 120 Hz.Nintendo Tech Specs Steam Deck + official dockDisplayPort 1.4, HDMI 2.0Up to 4K 60 Hz or 1440p 120 Hz; FreeSync (VRR).Valve dock specs ROG Xbox Ally X (2025)1× USB4 Type-C (Thunderbolt 4 compliance, DisplayPort 1.4 with FreeSync, PD 3.0); 1× USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C with DisplayPortUNKNOWN: maximum external resolution/refresh not stated.ASUS spec ROG Xbox Ally (2025)2× USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C with DisplayPort and power deliveryUNKNOWN: DisplayPort version and maximum external modes not stated.ASUS spec Lenovo Legion Go 8AHP2 / 8ASP22× USB-C (USB4 40Gbps) with DisplayPort 1.4 (8AHP2, Ryzen Z2) or DisplayPort 2.1 (8ASP2, Ryzen Z2 Extreme); the 2× USB-C listed as charging only are on the controllersUNKNOWN: maximum external modes not stated in PSREF.PSREF 8AHP2 · PSREF 8ASP2 Other handheld models (for example the original ROG Ally or Legion Go, or Legion Go S) were not checked: UNKNOWN. Use your model's spec page. Common wrong advice, corrected by the makers Wrong: "Xbox can't do 120 Hz at all without HDMI 2.1."Right: Xbox Support: on Series S or a TV without HDMI 2.1 you can still set 120 Hz at a lower resolution. If a mode both devices support is missing, Video fidelity & overscan → Overrides → HDMI lets you pick it (it reverts after 20 s if the TV rejects it). Source: Xbox Support, checked 2026-10-18. Wrong: "My monitor is 165 Hz, so the console will get 120 Hz."Right: Microsoft: some monitors support 120 Hz over DisplayPort but not over HDMI, and Xbox outputs HDMI. Check the HDMI input limits. Source: Xbox Support, checked 2026-10-18. Wrong: "Any USB-C charger or the old Switch adapter works on the Switch 2 dock."Right: Nintendo: HAC-002 cannot power the dock. Use NGN-01 or an adapter and cable with at least 54W. Source: Nintendo Support, checked 2026-10-18. Wrong: "A cheap DisplayPort-to-HDMI adapter is fine for the Steam Deck dock."Right: Valve: passive DP-to-HDMI adapters are not supported. Use an active adapter. Source: Steam Support, checked 2026-10-18. Wrong: "If the box says HDMI 2.1, the cable is fine."Right: HDMI Licensing Administrator: look for the Ultra High Speed HDMI Cable Certification Label (scannable QR) and the cable name on the jacket. Resellers may use other marketing terms. Source: HDMI LA, checked 2026-10-18. Wrong: "Putting the receiver in the chain can't hurt."Right: PlayStation lists a receiver or other intermediary equipment as a 4K 120 Hz cause. Microsoft says VRR may cause display issues through an AVR and suggests bypassing it. Source: PlayStation · Xbox Support, checked 2026-10-18. Wrong: "A factory reset is the first step for a black screen."Right: It is not the first step. Start with the display-only recovery above. Microsoft and PlayStation both offer a low-resolution or Change Video Output route first; PlayStation warns that some Safe Mode options delete data. Source: PlayStation Safe Mode · Xbox Support, checked 2026-10-18. Deep guides per device For a laptop or dock chain instead of a console HDMI path, use the Display & Connection Solver. Display & Connection Solver (PC / dock chains) PS5 HDMI 2.1 cable path (4K 120, VRR, when the supplied cable is enough) PS5 → 1440p monitor (HDMI vs DisplayPort limits) PS5 → Dell U2725QE (exact-pair example) Xbox Series X|S display compatibility (VRR order, Allow 4K, 1440p 120) Nintendo Switch 2 display path (dock HDMI, not USB-C Alt Mode) Steam Deck external display (direct cable vs official dock) Console → AVR / HDMI passthrough (direct TV + eARC first) HDMI capture / passthrough (only if you record or stream) USB-C hub vs dock (for Windows handhelds) USB-C PD charger compatibility Check the full path in the Compatibility EnginePick your console and display; the Engine keeps play-only paths direct and never adds capture hardware you don't need. PS5 → HDMI display → Xbox → HDMI display → Switch 2 → HDMI display → Handheld → HDMI display → FAQ How do I get a picture back when my console shows no signal?Use the maker's recovery route. Xbox Series X: hold Power + Eject until the second beep to start at 640 x 480. Xbox Series S: hold the Xbox button + Pair. PS5: start Safe Mode and choose Change Video Output. Steam Deck: turn on External display safe mode in the Display menu before docking. For Switch 2, Nintendo's no-video page starts with the dock power adapter (NGN-01, or at least 54W) and an Ultra High Speed HDMI cable; we found no documented low-resolution mode. Can Xbox run 120 Hz without HDMI 2.1?Yes, at a lower resolution. Microsoft's 'Set up 4K gaming at 120 Hz' article says that on a Series S, or a TV without HDMI 2.1, you can set Refresh rate to 120 Hz and the console lowers the resolution. The display must support 120 Hz over HDMI. For 4K at 120 Hz, Microsoft's articles disagree: 'Set up 4K gaming at 120 Hz' lists an Xbox Series X, an Ultra High Speed HDMI cable that supports HDMI 2.1 and an HDMI 2.1 TV, and says Series S owners who wish to game in 4K@120Hz need a certified Ultra High Speed HDMI cable; 'How to change the TV display settings' says 120Hz is only available for 1080p and 1440p. My monitor is 144 Hz. Why does my console not offer 120 Hz?Xbox sends video over HDMI, and Microsoft states that some monitors support 120 Hz over DisplayPort but not over HDMI. Check the monitor's HDMI input limits, not the DisplayPort headline number. Can I use my old Nintendo Switch adapter with the Switch 2 dock?No. Nintendo says the original Switch AC adapter (HAC-002) can power the Switch 2 console directly but cannot provide enough power for the dock. Use the Switch 2 adapter (NGN-01) or another adapter and cable with at least 54W. Does any DisplayPort-to-HDMI adapter work with the Steam Deck dock?No. Valve says passive DisplayPort-to-HDMI adapters are not supported and may cause issues. Use an active cable or adapter. What is the maximum external refresh rate of the ROG Xbox Ally or Legion Go?UNKNOWN. The ASUS and Lenovo spec pages we checked list the USB-C ports and DisplayPort support but no maximum external resolution or refresh rate. We do not guess it. Common wrong advice, corrected by the makers Wrong: "Xbox can't do 120 Hz at all without HDMI 2.1."Right: Xbox Support: on Series S or a TV without HDMI 2.1 you can still set 120 Hz at a lower resolution. If a mode both devices support is missing, Video fidelity & overscan → Overrides → HDMI lets you pick it (it reverts after 20 s if the TV rejects it). Source: Xbox Support, checked 2026-10-18. Wrong: "My monitor is 165 Hz, so the console will get 120 Hz."Right: Microsoft: some monitors support 120 Hz over DisplayPort but not over HDMI, and Xbox outputs HDMI. Check the HDMI input limits. Source: Xbox Support, checked 2026-10-18. Wrong: "Any USB-C charger or the old Switch adapter works on the Switch 2 dock."Right: Nintendo: HAC-002 cannot power the dock. Use NGN-01 or an adapter and cable with at least 54W. Source: Nintendo Support, checked 2026-10-18. Wrong: "A cheap DisplayPort-to-HDMI adapter is fine for the Steam Deck dock."Right: Valve: passive DP-to-HDMI adapters are not supported. Use an active adapter. Source: Steam Support, checked 2026-10-18. Wrong: "If the box says HDMI 2.1, the cable is fine."Right: HDMI Licensing Administrator: look for the Ultra High Speed HDMI Cable Certification Label (scannable QR) and the cable name on the jacket. Resellers may use other marketing terms. Source: HDMI LA, checked 2026-10-18. Wrong: "Putting the receiver in the chain can't hurt."Right: PlayStation lists a receiver or other intermediary equipment as a 4K 120 Hz cause. Microsoft says VRR may cause display issues through an AVR and suggests bypassing it. Source: PlayStation · Xbox Support, checked 2026-10-18. Wrong: "A factory reset is the first step for a black screen."Right: It is not the first step. Start with the display-only recovery above. Microsoft and PlayStation both offer a low-resolution or Change Video Output route first; PlayStation warns that some Safe Mode options delete data. Source: PlayStation Safe Mode · Xbox Support, checked 2026-10-18. Deep guides per device For a laptop or dock chain instead of a console HDMI path, use the Display & Connection Solver. PS5 → HDMI display → Xbox → HDMI display → Switch 2 → HDMI display → Handheld → HDMI display → FAQ How do I get a picture back when my console shows no signal?Use the maker's recovery route. Xbox Series X: hold Power + Eject until the second beep to start at 640 x 480. Xbox Series S: hold the Xbox button + Pair. PS5: start Safe Mode and choose Change Video Output. Steam Deck: turn on External display safe mode in the Display menu before docking. For Switch 2, Nintendo's no-video page starts with the dock power adapter (NGN-01, or at least 54W) and an Ultra High Speed HDMI cable; we found no documented low-resolution mode. Can Xbox run 120 Hz without HDMI 2.1?Yes, at a lower resolution. Microsoft's 'Set up 4K gaming at 120 Hz' article says that on a Series S, or a TV without HDMI 2.1, you can set Refresh rate to 120 Hz and the console lowers the resolution. The display must support 120 Hz over HDMI. For 4K at 120 Hz, Microsoft's articles disagree: 'Set up 4K gaming at 120 Hz' lists an Xbox Series X, an Ultra High Speed HDMI cable that supports HDMI 2.1 and an HDMI 2.1 TV, and says Series S owners who wish to game in 4K@120Hz need a certified Ultra High Speed HDMI cable; 'How to change the TV display settings' says 120Hz is only available for 1080p and 1440p. My monitor is 144 Hz. Why does my console not offer 120 Hz?Xbox sends video over HDMI, and Microsoft states that some monitors support 120 Hz over DisplayPort but not over HDMI. Check the monitor's HDMI input limits, not the DisplayPort headline number. Can I use my old Nintendo Switch adapter with the Switch 2 dock?No. Nintendo says the original Switch AC adapter (HAC-002) can power the Switch 2 console directly but cannot provide enough power for the dock. Use the Switch 2 adapter (NGN-01) or another adapter and cable with at least 54W. Does any DisplayPort-to-HDMI adapter work with the Steam Deck dock?No. Valve says passive DisplayPort-to-HDMI adapters are not supported and may cause issues. Use an active cable or adapter. What is the maximum external refresh rate of the ROG Xbox Ally or Legion Go?UNKNOWN. The ASUS and Lenovo spec pages we checked list the USB-C ports and DisplayPort support but no maximum external resolution or refresh rate. We do not guess it. Record/capture intent: play-only console→TV paths do not need a capture card; capture requires HDMI (or similar) loop/in hardware when you record or stream from the source.

main.domText: PC troubleshooting · BIOS accessCan’t enter BIOS but Windows starts? Fast Boot troubleshooterIf your PC boots straight into Windows and Delete or F2 never opens BIOS setup, one possible cause is the board’s firmware Fast Boot setting; a wireless keyboard, a USB port that starts late, or Windows Fast Startup after Shut down can also get in the way. This page separates that problem from a PC that does not POST or a PC that does not reach Windows, explains firmware Fast Boot vs Windows Fast Startup, and walks you through safe, manual next steps. Updated: 2026-10-18 Short answer: first try Windows’ own route into firmware: Settings → System → Recovery → Advanced startup → Restart now → Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings. On a Gigabyte board where that and the setup keys fail, Gigabyte’s Windows-based Fast Boot utility can offer an “Enter BIOS Setup Now” option. That route is testet på denne konfiguration (tested on this configuration) by one user on a Gigabyte B550I AORUS PRO AX rev 1.0. It is not a universal fix.Confidence: one user-tested configuration • no ELORUMTECH hardware reproduction • other boards unverified Interactive checkAnswer what you know. The result updates as you choose; “I don’t know yet” always gives an unknown result, never a pass. Nothing here runs, downloads, restarts or changes anything on your PC. 1. What happens when you power on? Windows starts normally, but I can’t open BIOS setup Nothing: no logo, no picture, no Windows (no POST) I see the board logo or firmware, but Windows doesn’t start2. Who made the motherboard? Gigabyte / AORUS Another maker I don’t know yet3. Which Gigabyte board? B550I AORUS PRO AX Another Gigabyte model I don’t know yet4. Board revision (printed on the board, e.g. “REV 1.0”) Rev 1.0 Another revision (I know which) I don’t know yet5. Windows version Windows 11 64-bit Windows 10 64-bit Something else (not 64-bit Windows 10/11) I don’t know yet6. Does Gigabyte’s support page for your exact board and revision list Fast Boot under Utility for your Windows version? Yes, it is listed No, it is not listed I haven’t checked7. After downloading: is the setup file validly signed by GIGA-BYTE TECHNOLOGY CO., LTD.? Yes, signature OK and signer is GIGA-BYTE TECHNOLOGY CO., LTD. No: invalid, missing or another signer Not checked yet Tested board · Windows 11 not testedTested board, but on Windows 11: start with GIGABYTE's page for your boardOn this configuration, one user's only working fix was Gigabyte Fast Boot utility B20.0420.1 → "Enter BIOS Setup Now" (testet på denne konfiguration). This is user testimony, not a guarantee: the Windows and BIOS versions in that test were not recorded.Windows 11 on the tested board: start with GIGABYTE: search your exact motherboard and revision in the GIGABYTE Download Center (first link below) or open GIGABYTE's own B550I AORUS PRO AX (Rev. 1.0) support page (second link), open Utility and check GIGABYTE's page for a Windows 11 version of Fast Boot. The Softpedia page linked last is a tested-case reference only (B20.0420.1, and its URL names Windows 10 64-bit). The owner of the tested PC confirmed on 2026-10-18 that this Softpedia page has the same program version for her board. We could not open the page, so its title, version, file name and supported OS are not verified by us. Read any prerequisite note (Gigabyte's Fast Boot listings note that APP Center must be installed first).Before running anything: right-click the setup file → Properties → Digital Signatures and confirm the signer is GIGA-BYTE TECHNOLOGY CO., LTD. and the signature is OK.Scan the downloaded file with your antivirus (for example Microsoft Defender) before running it.If Windows SmartScreen, User Account Control or your antivirus warns about the file or shows an unknown publisher, stop. Do not disable security or click past the warning.Save your work and close apps: entering BIOS setup restarts the PC, and the installer may also ask to restart.If BitLocker or device encryption is on, make sure you can find your recovery key before changing anything in BIOS setup.Install and open the utility yourself, then choose its option to enter BIOS setup (in the tested version: "Enter BIOS Setup Now") when you are ready. Nothing on this page runs, restarts or changes your PC.Results can differ with other BIOS versions, Windows versions or settings.The Softpedia link is for the tested configuration only. For any other board or revision, use the all-boards links.Per its URL, the Softpedia page is for Windows 10 64-bit, and the tested PC's Windows version was not recorded. On Windows 11, check GIGABYTE's page for your board for a Windows 11 version first.Search for your exact motherboard and revision (GIGABYTE Download Center): enter your model, choose the revision printed on the board, then open Utility → Fast Boot for your Windows version ↗ (external site)GIGABYTE B550I AORUS PRO AX (Rev. 1.0) support page (official): open Utility and look for Fast Boot for your Windows version ↗ (external site)Tested-case reference (B550I AORUS PRO AX rev 1.0 only): Softpedia page, B20.0420.1 per its URL ↗ (external site)Tested configuration only: Gigabyte B550I AORUS PRO AX rev 1.0. Per its URL, the page is for Windows 10 64-bit; we could not open it, so its contents are not verified by us. The tested PC's Windows version was not recorded. First: which problem do you have? Windows starts, but BIOS setup won’t openThe PC works and reaches Windows, yet the setup key never takes effect. This is the case this page is about. Firmware Fast Boot, a wireless keyboard, or a USB port that initialises late can all make the key press go unnoticed. No POST: nothing appears at allNo board logo, no picture and no Windows. That is a hardware or firmware start problem. A Windows utility cannot run, so check power and display cables and the board’s debug LEDs, and follow the no-POST section of your motherboard manual. Firmware starts, but Windows doesn’tYou see the logo but Windows never loads. Press the setup or boot-menu key repeatedly right after power-on, or use Windows Recovery (Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings) if it opens after failed starts. Firmware Fast Boot vs Windows Fast Startup Firmware Fast Boot is a motherboard setting. It shortens or skips hardware checks before Windows loads, which can leave almost no time to press the setup key. Windows Fast Startup is a Windows shutdown mode. Shut down saves the kernel session to a hibernation file so the next start is quicker. Microsoft documents that Fast Startup does not apply to Restart. When you are trying to reach firmware setup, use Restart rather than Shut down. The same Microsoft article notes that Fast Startup is enabled by default and that disabling it is not recommended. Boot-Escape ladder (safe order) Work top to bottom. This order follows Dell’s published paths and Microsoft’s firmware-handover command; Restart-vs-Shut-down and the wired keyboard come after the main methods, as in Dell’s troubleshooting section. Before you start: If you plan to change Secure Boot, TPM or boot mode, suspend BitLocker or have your recovery key ready. BitLocker can ask for the 48-digit recovery key after those firmware changes. Startup keys: Power on and tap the setup key from your board manual about once per second as soon as the logo appears (Delete and F2 are common; Dell documents F2 / F12). Windows handover: Settings → System → Recovery → Advanced startup → Restart now → Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings → Restart. Or from an admin terminal: shutdown /r /fw /t 0. If those fail: Restart again (not Shut down) so Fast Startup does not shorten the key window, and use a wired USB keyboard plugged into the PC (not a dock/hub). CMOS / clear-button last: Only as your board manual describes, with the PC unplugged. Do not start here. Sources for this ladder: Dell KB 000126121; Microsoft shutdown /fw; Microsoft Learn: boot to UEFI / common keys. Checked 2026-10-18. Why people open BIOS for Secure Boot / TPM Windows 11 requires UEFI firmware that is Secure Boot capable and a TPM 2.0. Secure Boot (with a TPM) is also what lets the firmware load only trusted OS bootloaders. Memory integrity and related virtualization-based security settings can require Secure Boot, and turning them off with a UEFI lock may need the firmware menus. That is a common reason to enter setup before installing Windows 11 or enabling those protections (some games’ anti-cheat requires Secure Boot and/or TPM 2.0 — for example EA Javelin / Secure Boot help, and Riot Vanguard’s TPM 2.0 requirement). Changing Secure Boot or TPM can trigger a BitLocker recovery-key prompt; suspend BitLocker first (Dell KB 000126121). Sources: Microsoft Learn: Windows 11 requirements (UEFI Secure Boot capable; TPM 2.0); Microsoft Learn: Secure the Windows boot process (Secure Boot + TPM; open firmware / Shift+Restart → UEFI Firmware settings); Microsoft Learn: TPM overview; Microsoft Learn: Memory integrity (UEFI BIOS / Secure Boot); EA Help: Secure Boot (“Some EA games require Secure Boot”); Riot Games Support: Enable TPM 2.0 (Vanguard); Dell KB 000126121 (suspend BitLocker before Secure Boot / TPM / boot-mode changes). Checked 2026-10-18. If “UEFI Firmware Settings” is missing or only restarts Dell’s guide lists three normal reasons why UEFI Firmware Settings is missing from Advanced options: the PC is running in legacy boot mode (Windows only shows the option when it started in UEFI mode; press Windows key + R, run msinfo32 and look at the BIOS Mode line, where “Legacy” explains it), the drive uses the older MBR partition style (UEFI mode needs a GPT drive), or the Windows Recovery Environment is turned off or damaged. Dell’s advice in that case is to use the startup keys instead, because they work whichever boot mode the PC uses (on Dell, F2 or F12). On other boards, use the setup key from your manual. Choose Restart rather than Shut down, since Fast Startup only affects Shut down, then press the key repeatedly as soon as the screen lights up. Microsoft lists Esc, Delete, F1, F2, F10, F11 and F12 as common keys and says to check your manufacturer’s site if the startup screen doesn’t show the key or goes by too fast. If the option is listed but the PC just restarts into Windows, neither source documents a specific cause. Fall back to the same route: a full Restart, then the setup key. Tested case (user testimony): testet på denne konfiguration BoardGigabyte B550I AORUS PRO AX, rev 1.0 SymptomWindows starts, but BIOS setup could not be opened Did not help in this user’s caseDelete / F2 at startup; Windows restart to UEFI Firmware Settings; CMOS reset Worked in this user’s caseGigabyte Fast Boot utility B20.0420.1 (archive mb_utility_fast_boot_B20.0420.1.zip), option “Enter BIOS Setup Now” Windows versionPer its URL, the Softpedia page is for Windows 10 64-bit; the tested PC’s Windows version was not recorded. BIOS versionNot recorded Evidence typeUser testimony. ELORUMTECH has not reproduced this on hardware. The methods that failed here are this user’s history, not proof they fail for everyone. Microsoft and Dell document the setup keys and the Windows restart to UEFI Firmware Settings as standard ways into firmware setup (see Sources). The tested file: how to tell if yours is the same We inspected the owner’s archive without running it. The setup.exe rows below are from our static inspection of the owner’s archive (not a malware scan or Windows/SmartScreen evaluation). If the SHA-256 of your download matches, it is byte-for-byte the same archive. A matching hash proves identity only. It does not prove the file is safe or that it suits your board. main.text: PC troubleshooting · BIOS accessCan’t enter BIOS but Windows starts? Fast Boot troubleshooterIf your PC boots straight into Windows and Delete or F2 never opens BIOS setup, one possible cause is the board’s firmware Fast Boot setting; a wireless keyboard, a USB port that starts late, or Windows Fast Startup after Shut down can also get in the way. This page separates that problem from a PC that does not POST or a PC that does not reach Windows, explains firmware Fast Boot vs Windows Fast Startup, and walks you through safe, manual next steps. Updated: 2026-10-18 Short answer: first try Windows’ own route into firmware: Settings → System → Recovery → Advanced startup → Restart now → Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings. On a Gigabyte board where that and the setup keys fail, Gigabyte’s Windows-based Fast Boot utility can offer an “Enter BIOS Setup Now” option. That route is testet på denne konfiguration (tested on this configuration) by one user on a Gigabyte B550I AORUS PRO AX rev 1.0. It is not a universal fix.Confidence: one user-tested configuration • no ELORUMTECH hardware reproduction • other boards unverified Interactive checkAnswer what you know. The result updates as you choose; “I don’t know yet” always gives an unknown result, never a pass. Nothing here runs, downloads, restarts or changes anything on your PC. 1. Per its URL, the page is for Windows 10 64-bit; we could not open it, so its contents are not verified by us. The tested PC's Windows version was not recorded. First: which problem do you have? Windows starts, but BIOS setup won’t openThe PC works and reaches Windows, yet the setup key never takes effect. This is the case this page is about. Firmware Fast Boot, a wireless keyboard, or a USB port that initialises late can all make the key press go unnoticed. No POST: nothing appears at allNo board logo, no picture and no Windows. That is a hardware or firmware start problem. A Windows utility cannot run, so check power and display cables and the board’s debug LEDs, and follow the no-POST section of your motherboard manual. Firmware starts, but Windows doesn’tYou see the logo but Windows never loads. Press the setup or boot-menu key repeatedly right after power-on, or use Windows Recovery (Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings) if it opens after failed starts. Firmware Fast Boot vs Windows Fast Startup Firmware Fast Boot is a motherboard setting. It shortens or skips hardware checks before Windows loads, which can leave almost no time to press the setup key. Windows Fast Startup is a Windows shutdown mode. Shut down saves the kernel session to a hibernation file so the next start is quicker. Microsoft documents that Fast Startup does not apply to Restart. When you are trying to reach firmware setup, use Restart rather than Shut down. The same Microsoft article notes that Fast Startup is enabled by default and that disabling it is not recommended. Boot-Escape ladder (safe order) Work top to bottom. This order follows Dell’s published paths and Microsoft’s firmware-handover command; Restart-vs-Shut-down and the wired keyboard come after the main methods, as in Dell’s troubleshooting section. Before you start: If you plan to change Secure Boot, TPM or boot mode, suspend BitLocker or have your recovery key ready. BitLocker can ask for the 48-digit recovery key after those firmware changes. Startup keys: Power on and tap the setup key from your board manual about once per second as soon as the logo appears (Delete and F2 are common; Dell documents F2 / F12). Windows handover: Settings → System → Recovery → Advanced startup → Restart now → Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings → Restart. Or from an admin terminal: shutdown /r /fw /t 0. If those fail: Restart again (not Shut down) so Fast Startup does not shorten the key window, and use a wired USB keyboard plugged into the PC (not a dock/hub). CMOS / clear-button last: Only as your board manual describes, with the PC unplugged. Do not start here. Sources for this ladder: Dell KB 000126121; Microsoft shutdown /fw; Microsoft Learn: boot to UEFI / common keys. Checked 2026-10-18. Why people open BIOS for Secure Boot / TPM Windows 11 requires UEFI firmware that is Secure Boot capable and a TPM 2.0. Secure Boot (with a TPM) is also what lets the firmware load only trusted OS bootloaders. Memory integrity and related virtualization-based security settings can require Secure Boot, and turning them off with a UEFI lock may need the firmware menus. That is a common reason to enter setup before installing Windows 11 or enabling those protections (some games’ anti-cheat requires Secure Boot and/or TPM 2.0 — for example EA Javelin / Secure Boot help, and Riot Vanguard’s TPM 2.0 requirement). Changing Secure Boot or TPM can trigger a BitLocker recovery-key prompt; suspend BitLocker first (Dell KB 000126121). Sources: Microsoft Learn: Windows 11 requirements (UEFI Secure Boot capable; TPM 2.0); Microsoft Learn: Secure the Windows boot process (Secure Boot + TPM; open firmware / Shift+Restart → UEFI Firmware settings); Microsoft Learn: TPM overview; Microsoft Learn: Memory integrity (UEFI BIOS / Secure Boot); EA Help: Secure Boot (“Some EA games require Secure Boot”); Riot Games Support: Enable TPM 2.0 (Vanguard); Dell KB 000126121 (suspend BitLocker before Secure Boot / TPM / boot-mode changes). Checked 2026-10-18. If “UEFI Firmware Settings” is missing or only restarts Dell’s guide lists three normal reasons why UEFI Firmware Settings is missing from Advanced options: the PC is running in legacy boot mode (Windows only shows the option when it started in UEFI mode; press Windows key + R, run msinfo32 and look at the BIOS Mode line, where “Legacy” explains it), the drive uses the older MBR partition style (UEFI mode needs a GPT drive), or the Windows Recovery Environment is turned off or damaged. Dell’s advice in that case is to use the startup keys instead, because they work whichever boot mode the PC uses (on Dell, F2 or F12). On other boards, use the setup key from your manual. Choose Restart rather than Shut down, since Fast Startup only affects Shut down, then press the key repeatedly as soon as the screen lights up. Microsoft lists Esc, Delete, F1, F2, F10, F11 and F12 as common keys and says to check your manufacturer’s site if the startup screen doesn’t show the key or goes by too fast. If the option is listed but the PC just restarts into Windows, neither source documents a specific cause. Fall back to the same route: a full Restart, then the setup key. First: which problem do you have? Windows starts, but BIOS setup won’t openThe PC works and reaches Windows, yet the setup key never takes effect. This is the case this page is about. Firmware Fast Boot, a wireless keyboard, or a USB port that initialises late can all make the key press go unnoticed. No POST: nothing appears at allNo board logo, no picture and no Windows. That is a hardware or firmware start problem. A Windows utility cannot run, so check power and display cables and the board’s debug LEDs, and follow the no-POST section of your motherboard manual. Firmware starts, but Windows doesn’tYou see the logo but Windows never loads. Press the setup or boot-menu key repeatedly right after power-on, or use Windows Recovery (Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings) if it opens after failed starts. Firmware Fast Boot vs Windows Fast Startup Firmware Fast Boot is a motherboard setting. It shortens or skips hardware checks before Windows loads, which can leave almost no time to press the setup key. Windows Fast Startup is a Windows shutdown mode. Shut down saves the kernel session to a hibernation file so the next start is quicker. Microsoft documents that Fast Startup does not apply to Restart. When you are trying to reach firmware setup, use Restart rather than Shut down. The same Microsoft article notes that Fast Startup is enabled by default and that disabling it is not recommended. Boot-Escape ladder (safe order) Work top to bottom. This order follows Dell’s published paths and Microsoft’s firmware-handover command; Restart-vs-Shut-down and the wired keyboard come after the main methods, as in Dell’s troubleshooting section. Before you start: If you plan to change Secure Boot, TPM or boot mode, suspend BitLocker or have your recovery key ready. BitLocker can ask for the 48-digit recovery key after those firmware changes. Startup keys: Power on and tap the setup key from your board manual about once per second as soon as the logo appears (Delete and F2 are common; Dell documents F2 / F12). Windows handover: Settings → System → Recovery → Advanced startup → Restart now → Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings → Restart. Or from an admin terminal: shutdown /r /fw /t 0. If those fail: Restart again (not Shut down) so Fast Startup does not shorten the key window, and use a wired USB keyboard plugged into the PC (not a dock/hub). CMOS / clear-button last: Only as your board manual describes, with the PC unplugged. Do not start here. Sources for this ladder: Dell KB 000126121; Microsoft shutdown /fw; Microsoft Learn: boot to UEFI / common keys. Checked 2026-10-18. Why people open BIOS for Secure Boot / TPM Windows 11 requires UEFI firmware that is Secure Boot capable and a TPM 2.0. Secure Boot (with a TPM) is also what lets the firmware load only trusted OS bootloaders. Memory integrity and related virtualization-based security settings can require Secure Boot, and turning them off with a UEFI lock may need the firmware menus. That is a common reason to enter setup before installing Windows 11 or enabling those protections (some games’ anti-cheat requires Secure Boot and/or TPM 2.0 — for example EA Javelin / Secure Boot help, and Riot Vanguard’s TPM 2.0 requirement). Changing Secure Boot or TPM can trigger a BitLocker recovery-key prompt; suspend BitLocker first (Dell KB 000126121). Dell’s advice in that case is to use the startup keys instead, because they work whichever boot mode the PC uses (on Dell, F2 or F12). On other boards, use the setup key from your manual. Choose Restart rather than Shut down, since Fast Startup only affects Shut down, then press the key repeatedly as soon as the screen lights up. Microsoft lists Esc, Delete, F1, F2, F10, F11 and F12 as common keys and says to check your manufacturer’s site if the startup screen doesn’t show the key or goes by too fast. If the option is listed but the PC just restarts into Windows, neither source documents a specific cause. Fall back to the same route: a full Restart, then the setup key. Fast Boot troubleshooterIf your PC boots straight into Windows and Delete or F2 never opens BIOS setup, one possible cause is the board’s firmware Fast Boot setting; a wireless keyboard, a USB port that starts late, or Windows Fast Startup after Shut down can also get in the way. This page separates that problem from a PC that does not POST or a PC that does not reach Windows, explains firmware Fast Boot vs Windows Fast Startup, and walks you through safe, manual next steps. Updated: 2026-10-18 Short answer: first try Windows’ own route into firmware: Settings → System → Recovery → Advanced startup → Restart now → Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings. On a Gigabyte board where that and the setup keys fail, Gigabyte’s Windows-based Fast Boot utility can offer an “Enter BIOS Setup Now” option. That route is testet på denne konfiguration (tested on this configuration) by one user on a Gigabyte B550I AORUS PRO AX rev 1.0. First: which problem do you have? Windows starts, but BIOS setup won’t openThe PC works and reaches Windows, yet the setup key never takes effect. This is the case this page is about. Firmware Fast Boot, a wireless keyboard, or a USB port that initialises late can all make the key press go unnoticed. No POST: nothing appears at allNo board logo, no picture and no Windows. That is a hardware or firmware start problem. A Windows utility cannot run, so check power and display cables and the board’s debug LEDs, and follow the no-POST section of your motherboard manual. Firmware starts, but Windows doesn’tYou see the logo but Windows never loads. Press the setup or boot-menu key repeatedly right after power-on, or use Windows Recovery (Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings) if it opens after failed starts. Firmware Fast Boot vs Windows Fast Startup Firmware Fast Boot is a motherboard setting. It shortens or skips hardware checks before Windows loads, which can leave almost no time to press the setup key. Windows Fast Startup is a Windows shutdown mode. Shut down saves the kernel session to a hibernation file so the next start is quicker. Microsoft documents that Fast Startup does not apply to Restart. When you are trying to reach firmware setup, use Restart rather than Shut down. The same Microsoft article notes that Fast Startup is enabled by default and that disabling it is not recommended. Boot-Escape ladder (safe order) Work top to bottom. This order follows Dell’s published paths and Microsoft’s firmware-handover command; Restart-vs-Shut-down and the wired keyboard come after the main methods, as in Dell’s troubleshooting section. Before you start: If you plan to change Secure Boot, TPM or boot mode, suspend BitLocker or have your recovery key ready. BitLocker can ask for the 48-digit recovery key after those firmware changes. Startup keys: Power on and tap the setup key from your board manual about once per second as soon as the logo appears (Delete and F2 are common; Dell documents F2 / F12). Windows handover: Settings → System → Recovery → Advanced startup → Restart now → Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings → Restart. Or from an admin terminal: shutdown /r /fw /t 0. If those fail: Restart again (not Shut down) so Fast Startup does not shorten the key window, and use a wired USB keyboard plugged into the PC (not a dock/hub). CMOS / clear-button last: Only as your board manual describes, with the PC unplugged. Do not start here. Sources for this ladder: Dell KB 000126121; Microsoft shutdown /fw; Microsoft Learn: boot to UEFI / common keys. Checked 2026-10-18. Why people open BIOS for Secure Boot / TPM Windows 11 requires UEFI firmware that is Secure Boot capable and a TPM 2.0. Secure Boot (with a TPM) is also what lets the firmware load only trusted OS bootloaders. Memory integrity and related virtualization-based security settings can require Secure Boot, and turning them off with a UEFI lock may need the firmware menus. That is a common reason to enter setup before installing Windows 11 or enabling those protections (some games’ anti-cheat requires Secure Boot and/or TPM 2.0 — for example EA Javelin / Secure Boot help, and Riot Vanguard’s TPM 2.0 requirement). Changing Secure Boot or TPM can trigger a BitLocker recovery-key prompt; suspend BitLocker first (Dell KB 000126121). Checked 2026-10-18. If “UEFI Firmware Settings” is missing or only restarts Dell’s guide lists three normal reasons why UEFI Firmware Settings is missing from Advanced options: the PC is running in legacy boot mode (Windows only shows the option when it started in UEFI mode; press Windows key + R, run msinfo32 and look at the BIOS Mode line, where “Legacy” explains it), the drive uses the older MBR partition style (UEFI mode needs a GPT drive), or the Windows Recovery Environment is turned off or damaged. Dell’s advice in that case is to use the startup keys instead, because they work whichever boot mode the PC uses (on Dell, F2 or F12). On other boards, use the setup key from your manual. Choose Restart rather than Shut down, since Fast Startup only affects Shut down, then press the key repeatedly as soon as the screen lights up. Microsoft lists Esc, Delete, F1, F2, F10, F11 and F12 as common keys and says to check your manufacturer’s site if the startup screen doesn’t show the key or goes by too fast. If the option is listed but the PC just restarts into Windows, neither source documents a specific cause. Fall back to the same route: a full Restart, then the setup key. That is a hardware or firmware start problem. A Windows utility cannot run, so check power and display cables and the board’s debug LEDs, and follow the no-POST section of your motherboard manual. Firmware starts, but Windows doesn’tYou see the logo but Windows never loads. Press the setup or boot-menu key repeatedly right after power-on, or use Windows Recovery (Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings) if it opens after failed starts. Firmware Fast Boot vs Windows Fast Startup Firmware Fast Boot is a motherboard setting. It shortens or skips hardware checks before Windows loads, which can leave almost no time to press the setup key. Windows Fast Startup is a Windows shutdown mode. Shut down saves the kernel session to a hibernation file so the next start is quicker. Microsoft documents that Fast Startup does not apply to Restart. When you are trying to reach firmware setup, use Restart rather than Shut down. The same Microsoft article notes that Fast Startup is enabled by default and that disabling it is not recommended. Boot-Escape ladder (safe order) Work top to bottom. This order follows Dell’s published paths and Microsoft’s firmware-handover command; Restart-vs-Shut-down and the wired keyboard come after the main methods, as in Dell’s troubleshooting section. Before you start: If you plan to change Secure Boot, TPM or boot mode, suspend BitLocker or have your recovery key ready. BitLocker can ask for the 48-digit recovery key after those firmware changes. Startup keys: Power on and tap the setup key from your board manual about once per second as soon as the logo appears (Delete and F2 are common; Dell documents F2 / F12). Windows handover: Settings → System → Recovery → Advanced startup → Restart now → Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings → Restart. Or from an admin terminal: shutdown /r /fw /t 0. If those fail: Restart again (not Shut down) so Fast Startup does not shorten the key window, and use a wired USB keyboard plugged into the PC (not a dock/hub). CMOS / clear-button last: Only as your board manual describes, with the PC unplugged. Do not start here. Sources for this ladder: Dell KB 000126121; Microsoft shutdown /fw; Microsoft Learn: boot to UEFI / common keys. Checked 2026-10-18. Why people open BIOS for Secure Boot / TPM Windows 11 requires UEFI firmware that is Secure Boot capable and a TPM 2.0. Secure Boot (with a TPM) is also what lets the firmware load only trusted OS bootloaders. Memory integrity and related virtualization-based security settings can require Secure Boot, and turning them off with a UEFI lock may need the firmware menus. That is a common reason to enter setup before installing Windows 11 or enabling those protections (some games’ anti-cheat requires Secure Boot and/or TPM 2.0 — for example EA Javelin / Secure Boot help, and Riot Vanguard’s TPM 2.0 requirement). Changing Secure Boot or TPM can trigger a BitLocker recovery-key prompt; suspend BitLocker first (Dell KB 000126121). Sources: Microsoft Learn: Windows 11 requirements (UEFI Secure Boot capable; TPM 2.0); Microsoft Learn: Secure the Windows boot process (Secure Boot + TPM; open firmware / Shift+Restart → UEFI Firmware settings); Microsoft Learn: TPM overview; Microsoft Learn: Memory integrity (UEFI BIOS / Secure Boot); EA Help: Secure Boot (“Some EA games require Secure Boot”); Riot Games Support: Enable TPM 2.0 (Vanguard); Dell KB 000126121 (suspend BitLocker before Secure Boot / TPM / boot-mode changes). Checked 2026-10-18. If “UEFI Firmware Settings” is missing or only restarts Dell’s guide lists three normal reasons why UEFI Firmware Settings is missing from Advanced options: the PC is running in legacy boot mode (Windows only shows the option when it started in UEFI mode; press Windows key + R, run msinfo32 and look at the BIOS Mode line, where “Legacy” explains it), the drive uses the older MBR partition style (UEFI mode needs a GPT drive), or the Windows Recovery Environment is turned off or damaged. Dell’s advice in that case is to use the startup keys instead, because they work whichever boot mode the PC uses (on Dell, F2 or F12). On other boards, use the setup key from your manual. Choose Restart rather than Shut down, since Fast Startup only affects Shut down, then press the key repeatedly as soon as the screen lights up. Microsoft lists Esc, Delete, F1, F2, F10, F11 and F12 as common keys and says to check your manufacturer’s site if the startup screen doesn’t show the key or goes by too fast. If the option is listed but the PC just restarts into Windows, neither source documents a specific cause. Fall back to the same route: a full Restart, then the setup key. The signer should be GIGA-BYTE TECHNOLOGY CO., LTD. and the signature should be OK.Scan the file with your antivirus, for example Microsoft Defender.If Windows SmartScreen, User Account Control or your antivirus warns or shows an unknown publisher, stop. ELORUMTECH never flashes BIOS, resets CMOS, restarts your PC or runs installers. Common wrong advice Wrong: “Turn off Fast Startup in Windows Power Options — that is the same as Fast Boot.”Right: Windows Fast Startup is a Windows shutdown mode (Power Options / shutdown /hybrid). Firmware Fast Boot is a motherboard BIOS setting (for example ASUS Boot → Fast Boot). They live in different places and fix different problems. Sources: Dell KB 000126121 (Fast Startup in Power Options; affects Shut down, not Restart); ASUS FAQ 1044641 (disable Fast Boot in BIOS); Microsoft shutdown (/hybrid vs /fw), checked 2026-10-18. Wrong: “If Delete/F2 never opens setup, clear CMOS first.”Right: Dell’s guide uses F2/F12 at startup, Windows Advanced startup → UEFI Firmware Settings or shutdown /r /fw /t 0 (admin terminal), and, if that fails, Restart instead of Shut down and a wired keyboard. It does not include clearing CMOS. Sources: Dell KB 000126121; ASUS FAQ 1008829 (Advanced startup → UEFI Firmware Settings); Microsoft shutdown /fw, checked 2026-10-18. FAQWhy can’t I enter BIOS even though Windows starts?With firmware Fast Boot enabled, the board can skip or shorten the moment where it reads the setup key, so Delete or F2 may never register. Wireless keyboards and some USB ports can also be ignored that early. Try the Windows route first: Settings → System → Recovery → Advanced startup → Restart now → Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings.Is firmware Fast Boot the same as Windows Fast Startup?No. Firmware Fast Boot is a motherboard setting that shortens hardware checks before Windows loads. Windows Fast Startup is a Windows shutdown mode that saves the kernel session to disk so the next start is faster. Microsoft notes that Fast Startup does not apply to Restart, so use Restart (not Shut down) when you try to reach firmware setup.Did the Gigabyte Fast Boot utility work for everyone?We only know one case. On a Gigabyte B550I AORUS PRO AX rev 1.0, one user reports that Fast Boot utility B20.0420.1 with “Enter BIOS Setup Now” was the only thing that worked. That is user testimony on that configuration, not a guarantee for other boards, revisions, BIOS versions or Windows versions.Where should I download the Fast Boot utility?For any board: search your exact motherboard and revision in the GIGABYTE Download Center and use the Utility section. Only for the tested Gigabyte B550I AORUS PRO AX rev 1.0, this page also links a Softpedia page as a tested-case reference. The owner of the tested PC confirmed on 2026-10-18 that this Softpedia page has the same program version for her board. We could not open the page, so its title, version, file name and supported OS are not verified by us. Per its URL, the Softpedia page is for Windows 10 64-bit; the tested PC’s Windows version was not recorded. ELORUMTECH does not host the file. Never use a Fast Boot file made for another board.How do I check that the file is genuine?Right-click the setup file → Properties → Digital Signatures and confirm the signer is GIGA-BYTE TECHNOLOGY CO., LTD. and the signature is OK, then scan it with your antivirus. If Windows SmartScreen, User Account Control or your antivirus warns, stop. Do not disable security or click past the warning.What if my PC shows nothing at all when I press power?That is a no-POST problem, not a BIOS-access problem. A Windows utility cannot help because Windows never starts. Check power and display cables and the board’s debug LEDs, and follow the no-POST section of your motherboard manual. Fast Boot troubleshooterIf your PC boots straight into Windows and Delete or F2 never opens BIOS setup, one possible cause is the board’s firmware Fast Boot setting; a wireless keyboard, a USB port that starts late, or Windows Fast Startup after Shut down can also get in the way. This page separates that problem from a PC that does not POST or a PC that does not reach Windows, explains firmware Fast Boot vs Windows Fast Startup, and walks you through safe, manual next steps. On a Gigabyte board where that and the setup keys fail, Gigabyte’s Windows-based Fast Boot utility can offer an “Enter BIOS Setup Now” option. That route is testet på denne konfiguration (tested on this configuration) by one user on a Gigabyte B550I AORUS PRO AX rev 1.0. main.text: PC troubleshooting · BIOS accessCan’t enter BIOS but Windows starts? Fast Boot troubleshooterIf your PC boots straight into Windows and Delete or F2 never opens BIOS setup, one possible cause is the board’s firmware Fast Boot setting; a wireless keyboard, a USB port that starts late, or Windows Fast Startup after Shut down can also get in the way. This page separates that problem from a PC that does not POST or a PC that does not reach Windows, explains firmware Fast Boot vs Windows Fast Startup, and walks you through safe, manual next steps. Updated: 2026-10-18 Short answer: first try Windows’ own route into firmware: Settings → System → Recovery → Advanced startup → Restart now → Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings. On a Gigabyte board where that and the setup keys fail, Gigabyte’s Windows-based Fast Boot utility can offer an “Enter BIOS Setup Now” option. That route is testet på denne konfiguration (tested on this configuration) by one user on a Gigabyte B550I AORUS PRO AX rev 1.0. It is not a universal fix.Confidence: one user-tested configuration • no ELORUMTECH hardware reproduction • other boards unverified Interactive checkAnswer what you know. The result updates as you choose; “I don’t know yet” always gives an unknown result, never a pass. Nothing here runs, downloads, restarts or changes anything on your PC. 1. First: which problem do you have? Windows starts, but BIOS setup won’t openThe PC works and reaches Windows, yet the setup key never takes effect. This is the case this page is about. Firmware Fast Boot, a wireless keyboard, or a USB port that initialises late can all make the key press go unnoticed. No POST: nothing appears at allNo board logo, no picture and no Windows. That is a hardware or firmware start problem. A Windows utility cannot run, so check power and display cables and the board’s debug LEDs, and follow the no-POST section of your motherboard manual. Firmware starts, but Windows doesn’tYou see the logo but Windows never loads. Press the setup or boot-menu key repeatedly right after power-on, or use Windows Recovery (Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings) if it opens after failed starts. Firmware Fast Boot vs Windows Fast Startup Firmware Fast Boot is a motherboard setting. It shortens or skips hardware checks before Windows loads, which can leave almost no time to press the setup key. Windows Fast Startup is a Windows shutdown mode. Shut down saves the kernel session to a hibernation file so the next start is quicker. Microsoft documents that Fast Startup does not apply to Restart. When you are trying to reach firmware setup, use Restart rather than Shut down. The same Microsoft article notes that Fast Startup is enabled by default and that disabling it is not recommended. Boot-Escape ladder (safe order) Work top to bottom. This order follows Dell’s published paths and Microsoft’s firmware-handover command; Restart-vs-Shut-down and the wired keyboard come after the main methods, as in Dell’s troubleshooting section. Before you start: If you plan to change Secure Boot, TPM or boot mode, suspend BitLocker or have your recovery key ready. BitLocker can ask for the 48-digit recovery key after those firmware changes. Startup keys: Power on and tap the setup key from your board manual about once per second as soon as the logo appears (Delete and F2 are common; Dell documents F2 / F12). Windows handover: Settings → System → Recovery → Advanced startup → Restart now → Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings → Restart. Or from an admin terminal: shutdown /r /fw /t 0. If those fail: Restart again (not Shut down) so Fast Startup does not shorten the key window, and use a wired USB keyboard plugged into the PC (not a dock/hub). CMOS / clear-button last: Only as your board manual describes, with the PC unplugged. Do not start here. Sources for this ladder: Dell KB 000126121; Microsoft shutdown /fw; Microsoft Learn: boot to UEFI / common keys. Checked 2026-10-18. Why people open BIOS for Secure Boot / TPM Windows 11 requires UEFI firmware that is Secure Boot capable and a TPM 2.0. Secure Boot (with a TPM) is also what lets the firmware load only trusted OS bootloaders. Memory integrity and related virtualization-based security settings can require Secure Boot, and turning them off with a UEFI lock may need the firmware menus. That is a common reason to enter setup before installing Windows 11 or enabling those protections (some games’ anti-cheat requires Secure Boot and/or TPM 2.0 — for example EA Javelin / Secure Boot help, and Riot Vanguard’s TPM 2.0 requirement). Changing Secure Boot or TPM can trigger a BitLocker recovery-key prompt; suspend BitLocker first (Dell KB 000126121). Choose Restart rather than Shut down, since Fast Startup only affects Shut down, then press the key repeatedly as soon as the screen lights up. Microsoft lists Esc, Delete, F1, F2, F10, F11 and F12 as common keys and says to check your manufacturer’s site if the startup screen doesn’t show the key or goes by too fast. If the option is listed but the PC just restarts into Windows, neither source documents a specific cause. Fall back to the same route: a full Restart, then the setup key. Firmware Fast Boot, a wireless keyboard, or a USB port that initialises late can all make the key press go unnoticed. No POST: nothing appears at allNo board logo, no picture and no Windows. That is a hardware or firmware start problem. A Windows utility cannot run, so check power and display cables and the board’s debug LEDs, and follow the no-POST section of your motherboard manual. Firmware starts, but Windows doesn’tYou see the logo but Windows never loads. Firmware Fast Boot vs Windows Fast Startup Firmware Fast Boot is a motherboard setting. It shortens or skips hardware checks before Windows loads, which can leave almost no time to press the setup key. Windows Fast Startup is a Windows shutdown mode. Shut down saves the kernel session to a hibernation file so the next start is quicker. Microsoft documents that Fast Startup does not apply to Restart. Boot-Escape ladder (safe order) Work top to bottom. Before you start: If you plan to change Secure Boot, TPM or boot mode, suspend BitLocker or have your recovery key ready. BitLocker can ask for the 48-digit recovery key after those firmware changes. Fast Boot troubleshooterIf your PC boots straight into Windows and Delete or F2 never opens BIOS setup, one possible cause is the board’s firmware Fast Boot setting; a wireless keyboard, a USB port that starts late, or Windows Fast Startup after Shut down can also get in the way. This page separates that problem from a PC that does not POST or a PC that does not reach Windows, explains firmware Fast Boot vs Windows Fast Startup, and walks you through safe, manual next steps. Use your board manual's firmware key or your OS's firmware-restart option. First: which problem do you have? Windows starts, but BIOS setup won’t openThe PC works and reaches Windows, yet the setup key never takes effect. This is the case this page is about. Firmware Fast Boot, a wireless keyboard, or a USB port that initialises late can all make the key press go unnoticed. No POST: nothing appears at allNo board logo, no picture and no Windows. That is a hardware or firmware start problem. A Windows utility cannot run, so check power and display cables and the board’s debug LEDs, and follow the no-POST section of your motherboard manual. Firmware starts, but Windows doesn’tYou see the logo but Windows never loads. Press the setup or boot-menu key repeatedly right after power-on, or use Windows Recovery (Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings) if it opens after failed starts. Firmware Fast Boot vs Windows Fast Startup Firmware Fast Boot is a motherboard setting. It shortens or skips hardware checks before Windows loads, which can leave almost no time to press the setup key. Windows Fast Startup is a Windows shutdown mode. Shut down saves the kernel session to a hibernation file so the next start is quicker. Microsoft documents that Fast Startup does not apply to Restart. When you are trying to reach firmware setup, use Restart rather than Shut down. The same Microsoft article notes that Fast Startup is enabled by default and that disabling it is not recommended. Boot-Escape ladder (safe order) Work top to bottom. This order follows Dell’s published paths and Microsoft’s firmware-handover command; Restart-vs-Shut-down and the wired keyboard come after the main methods, as in Dell’s troubleshooting section. Before you start: If you plan to change Secure Boot, TPM or boot mode, suspend BitLocker or have your recovery key ready. BitLocker can ask for the 48-digit recovery key after those firmware changes. Startup keys: Power on and tap the setup key from your board manual about once per second as soon as the logo appears (Delete and F2 are common; Dell documents F2 / F12). Windows handover: Settings → System → Recovery → Advanced startup → Restart now → Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings → Restart. Or from an admin terminal: shutdown /r /fw /t 0. If those fail: Restart again (not Shut down) so Fast Startup does not shorten the key window, and use a wired USB keyboard plugged into the PC (not a dock/hub). CMOS / clear-button last: Only as your board manual describes, with the PC unplugged. Do not start here. Sources for this ladder: Dell KB 000126121; Microsoft shutdown /fw; Microsoft Learn: boot to UEFI / common keys. Checked 2026-10-18. Why people open BIOS for Secure Boot / TPM Windows 11 requires UEFI firmware that is Secure Boot capable and a TPM 2.0. Secure Boot (with a TPM) is also what lets the firmware load only trusted OS bootloaders. Memory integrity and related virtualization-based security settings can require Secure Boot, and turning them off with a UEFI lock may need the firmware menus. That is a common reason to enter setup before installing Windows 11 or enabling those protections (some games’ anti-cheat requires Secure Boot and/or TPM 2.0 — for example EA Javelin / Secure Boot help, and Riot Vanguard’s TPM 2.0 requirement). Changing Secure Boot or TPM can trigger a BitLocker recovery-key prompt; suspend BitLocker first (Dell KB 000126121). Checked 2026-10-18. If “UEFI Firmware Settings” is missing or only restarts Dell’s guide lists three normal reasons why UEFI Firmware Settings is missing from Advanced options: the PC is running in legacy boot mode (Windows only shows the option when it started in UEFI mode; press Windows key + R, run msinfo32 and look at the BIOS Mode line, where “Legacy” explains it), the drive uses the older MBR partition style (UEFI mode needs a GPT drive), or the Windows Recovery Environment is turned off or damaged. Dell’s advice in that case is to use the startup keys instead, because they work whichever boot mode the PC uses (on Dell, F2 or F12). On other boards, use the setup key from your manual. Choose Restart rather than Shut down, since Fast Startup only affects Shut down, then press the key repeatedly as soon as the screen lights up. Microsoft lists Esc, Delete, F1, F2, F10, F11 and F12 as common keys and says to check your manufacturer’s site if the startup screen doesn’t show the key or goes by too fast. If the option is listed but the PC just restarts into Windows, neither source documents a specific cause. Fall back to the same route: a full Restart, then the setup key. Firmware starts, but Windows doesn’tYou see the logo but Windows never loads. main.text: PC troubleshooting · BIOS accessCan’t enter BIOS but Windows starts? Fast Boot troubleshooterIf your PC boots straight into Windows and Delete or F2 never opens BIOS setup, one possible cause is the board’s firmware Fast Boot setting; a wireless keyboard, a USB port that starts late, or Windows Fast Startup after Shut down can also get in the way. This page separates that problem from a PC that does not POST or a PC that does not reach Windows, explains firmware Fast Boot vs Windows Fast Startup, and walks you through safe, manual next steps. Updated: 2026-10-18 Short answer: first try Windows’ own route into firmware: Settings → System → Recovery → Advanced startup → Restart now → Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings. On a Gigabyte board where that and the setup keys fail, Gigabyte’s Windows-based Fast Boot utility can offer an “Enter BIOS Setup Now” option. That route is testet på denne konfiguration (tested on this configuration) by one user on a Gigabyte B550I AORUS PRO AX rev 1.0. It is not a universal fix.Confidence: one user-tested configuration • no ELORUMTECH hardware reproduction • other boards unverified Interactive checkAnswer what you know. The result updates as you choose; “I don’t know yet” always gives an unknown result, never a pass. Nothing here runs, downloads, restarts or changes anything on your PC. 1. No: invalid, missing or another signer Not checked yet Different problemNo POST: this is a hardware/firmware start problem, not a BIOS-access problemIf there is no firmware logo, no display output and no Windows, a Windows utility cannot run. Fast Boot settings are not the first suspect.Check power cables (24-pin and CPU power), display cable on the correct output, and any debug LEDs on the board.Follow your motherboard manual's no-POST / debug LED section.Clear CMOS only as described in your board manual, with the PC unplugged.Contact the motherboard manufacturer's support if the board still does not POST.Do not install or run boot utilities for this symptom. First: which problem do you have? Windows starts, but BIOS setup won’t openThe PC works and reaches Windows, yet the setup key never takes effect. This is the case this page is about. Firmware Fast Boot, a wireless keyboard, or a USB port that initialises late can all make the key press go unnoticed. No POST: nothing appears at allNo board logo, no picture and no Windows. That is a hardware or firmware start problem. A Windows utility cannot run, so check power and display cables and the board’s debug LEDs, and follow the no-POST section of your motherboard manual. Firmware starts, but Windows doesn’tYou see the logo but Windows never loads. Press the setup or boot-menu key repeatedly right after power-on, or use Windows Recovery (Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings) if it opens after failed starts. Firmware Fast Boot vs Windows Fast Startup Firmware Fast Boot is a motherboard setting. It shortens or skips hardware checks before Windows loads, which can leave almost no time to press the setup key. Windows Fast Startup is a Windows shutdown mode. Shut down saves the kernel session to a hibernation file so the next start is quicker. Microsoft documents that Fast Startup does not apply to Restart. When you are trying to reach firmware setup, use Restart rather than Shut down. The same Microsoft article notes that Fast Startup is enabled by default and that disabling it is not recommended. Boot-Escape ladder (safe order) Work top to bottom. This order follows Dell’s published paths and Microsoft’s firmware-handover command; Restart-vs-Shut-down and the wired keyboard come after the main methods, as in Dell’s troubleshooting section. Before you start: If you plan to change Secure Boot, TPM or boot mode, suspend BitLocker or have your recovery key ready. BitLocker can ask for the 48-digit recovery key after those firmware changes. Startup keys: Power on and tap the setup key from your board manual about once per second as soon as the logo appears (Delete and F2 are common; Dell documents F2 / F12). Windows handover: Settings → System → Recovery → Advanced startup → Restart now → Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings → Restart. Or from an admin terminal: shutdown /r /fw /t 0. If those fail: Restart again (not Shut down) so Fast Startup does not shorten the key window, and use a wired USB keyboard plugged into the PC (not a dock/hub). CMOS / clear-button last: Only as your board manual describes, with the PC unplugged. Do not start here. Sources for this ladder: Dell KB 000126121; Microsoft shutdown /fw; Microsoft Learn: boot to UEFI / common keys. Checked 2026-10-18. Why people open BIOS for Secure Boot / TPM Windows 11 requires UEFI firmware that is Secure Boot capable and a TPM 2.0. Secure Boot (with a TPM) is also what lets the firmware load only trusted OS bootloaders. Memory integrity and related virtualization-based security settings can require Secure Boot, and turning them off with a UEFI lock may need the firmware menus. That is a common reason to enter setup before installing Windows 11 or enabling those protections (some games’ anti-cheat requires Secure Boot and/or TPM 2.0 — for example EA Javelin / Secure Boot help, and Riot Vanguard’s TPM 2.0 requirement). Changing Secure Boot or TPM can trigger a BitLocker recovery-key prompt; suspend BitLocker first (Dell KB 000126121). Checked 2026-10-18. If “UEFI Firmware Settings” is missing or only restarts Dell’s guide lists three normal reasons why UEFI Firmware Settings is missing from Advanced options: the PC is running in legacy boot mode (Windows only shows the option when it started in UEFI mode; press Windows key + R, run msinfo32 and look at the BIOS Mode line, where “Legacy” explains it), the drive uses the older MBR partition style (UEFI mode needs a GPT drive), or the Windows Recovery Environment is turned off or damaged. Dell’s advice in that case is to use the startup keys instead, because they work whichever boot mode the PC uses (on Dell, F2 or F12). On other boards, use the setup key from your manual. Choose Restart rather than Shut down, since Fast Startup only affects Shut down, then press the key repeatedly as soon as the screen lights up. Microsoft lists Esc, Delete, F1, F2, F10, F11 and F12 as common keys and says to check your manufacturer’s site if the startup screen doesn’t show the key or goes by too fast. If the option is listed but the PC just restarts into Windows, neither source documents a specific cause. Fall back to the same route: a full Restart, then the setup key. main.domText: Home › Guides › Console & handheld display hub Console & handheld → TV / monitor Console & handheld display hub No signal, no 120 Hz, wrong resolution, or a receiver or dock that breaks the picture. Pick your device and symptom: you get the maker's own steps in a safe order, each with its source and the date we checked it. Where the maker publishes nothing, we say UNKNOWN instead of guessing. Updated: 2026-10-18 · Sources checked: 2026-10-18 Short answer: connect the console directly to the screen's HDMI input first and remove receivers, splitters and adapters. If the screen stays black, use the maker's low-resolution recovery (table below) instead of resetting the console. For 120 Hz, the screen must accept 120 Hz over HDMI; a monitor's DisplayPort refresh rate does not count for an HDMI path. Wrong: "My monitor is 165 Hz, so the console will get 120 Hz."Right: Microsoft: some monitors support 120 Hz over DisplayPort but not over HDMI, and Xbox outputs HDMI. Check the HDMI input limits. Source: Xbox Support, checked 2026-10-18. Wrong: "Any USB-C charger or the old Switch adapter works on the Switch 2 dock."Right: Nintendo: HAC-002 cannot power the dock. Wrong: "A cheap DisplayPort-to-HDMI adapter is fine for the Steam Deck dock."Right: Valve: passive DP-to-HDMI adapters are not supported. Use an active adapter. Source: Steam Support, checked 2026-10-18. Wrong: "If the box says HDMI 2.1, the cable is fine."Right: HDMI Licensing Administrator: look for the Ultra High Speed HDMI Cable Certification Label (scannable QR) and the cable name on the jacket. Xbox Series X: hold Power + Eject until the second beep to start at 640 x 480. Xbox Series S: hold the Xbox button + Pair. PS5: start Safe Mode and choose Change Video Output. Steam Deck: turn on External display safe mode in the Display menu before docking. Can Xbox run 120 Hz without HDMI 2.1?Yes, at a lower resolution. The ASUS and Lenovo spec pages we checked list the USB-C ports and DisplayPort support but no maximum external resolution or refresh rate. We do not guess it. Xbox Series X: hold Power + Eject until the second beep to start at 640 x 480. Xbox Series S: hold the Xbox button + Pair. PS5: start Safe Mode and choose Change Video Output. The display must support 120 Hz over HDMI. My monitor is 144 Hz. Why does my console not offer 120 Hz?Xbox sends video over HDMI, and Microsoft states that some monitors support 120 Hz over DisplayPort but not over HDMI. Check the monitor's HDMI input limits, not the DisplayPort headline number. Use the Switch 2 adapter (NGN-01) or another adapter and cable with at least 54W. Does any DisplayPort-to-HDMI adapter work with the Steam Deck dock?No. Valve says passive DisplayPort-to-HDMI adapters are not supported and may cause issues. Use an active cable or adapter. What is the maximum external refresh rate of the ROG Xbox Ally or Legion Go?UNKNOWN. The ASUS and Lenovo spec pages we checked list the USB-C ports and DisplayPort support but no maximum external resolution or refresh rate. We do not guess it. Does any DisplayPort-to-HDMI adapter work with the Steam Deck dock?No. Valve says passive DisplayPort-to-HDMI adapters are not supported and may cause issues. Use an active cable or adapter. What is the maximum external refresh rate of the ROG Xbox Ally or Legion Go?UNKNOWN. The ASUS and Lenovo spec pages we checked list the USB-C ports and DisplayPort support but no maximum external resolution or refresh rate. We do not guess it. Xbox Series X: hold Power + Eject until the second beep to start at 640 x 480. Xbox Series S: hold the Xbox button + Pair. PS5: start Safe Mode and choose Change Video Output. Steam Deck: turn on External display safe mode in the Display menu before docking. For Switch 2, Nintendo's no-video page starts with the dock power adapter (NGN-01, or at least 54W) and an Ultra High Speed HDMI cable; we found no documented low-resolution mode. Can Xbox run 120 Hz without HDMI 2.1?Yes, at a lower resolution. Microsoft's 'Set up 4K gaming at 120 Hz' article says that on a Series S, or a TV without HDMI 2.1, you can set Refresh rate to 120 Hz and the console lowers the resolution. The display must support 120 Hz over HDMI. For 4K at 120 Hz, Microsoft's articles disagree: 'Set up 4K gaming at 120 Hz' lists an Xbox Series X, an Ultra High Speed HDMI cable that supports HDMI 2.1 and an HDMI 2.1 TV, and says Series S owners who wish to game in 4K@120Hz need a certified Ultra High Speed HDMI cable; 'How to change the TV display settings' says 120Hz is only available for 1080p and 1440p. Check the monitor's HDMI input limits, not the DisplayPort headline number. Use the Switch 2 adapter (NGN-01) or another adapter and cable with at least 54W. Does any DisplayPort-to-HDMI adapter work with the Steam Deck dock?No. Valve says passive DisplayPort-to-HDMI adapters are not supported and may cause issues. Use an active cable or adapter. What is the maximum external refresh rate of the ROG Xbox Ally or Legion Go?UNKNOWN. The ASUS and Lenovo spec pages we checked list the USB-C ports and DisplayPort support but no maximum external resolution or refresh rate. We do not guess it. Wrong: "My monitor is 165 Hz, so the console will get 120 Hz."Right: Microsoft: some monitors support 120 Hz over DisplayPort but not over HDMI, and Xbox outputs HDMI. Check the HDMI input limits. Source: Xbox Support, checked 2026-10-18. Wrong: "Any USB-C charger or the old Switch adapter works on the Switch 2 dock."Right: Nintendo: HAC-002 cannot power the dock. Wrong: "A cheap DisplayPort-to-HDMI adapter is fine for the Steam Deck dock."Right: Valve: passive DP-to-HDMI adapters are not supported. Use an active adapter. Source: Steam Support, checked 2026-10-18. Wrong: "If the box says HDMI 2.1, the cable is fine."Right: HDMI Licensing Administrator: look for the Ultra High Speed HDMI Cable Certification Label (scannable QR) and the cable name on the jacket. Xbox Series X: hold Power + Eject until the second beep to start at 640 x 480. Xbox Series S: hold the Xbox button + Pair. PS5: start Safe Mode and choose Change Video Output. Steam Deck: turn on External display safe mode in the Display menu before docking. For Switch 2, Nintendo's no-video page starts with the dock power adapter (NGN-01, or at least 54W) and an Ultra High Speed HDMI cable; we found no documented low-resolution mode. Can Xbox run 120 Hz without HDMI 2.1?Yes, at a lower resolution. Microsoft's 'Set up 4K gaming at 120 Hz' article says that on a Series S, or a TV without HDMI 2.1, you can set Refresh rate to 120 Hz and the console lowers the resolution. The display must support 120 Hz over HDMI. For 4K at 120 Hz, Microsoft's articles disagree: 'Set up 4K gaming at 120 Hz' lists an Xbox Series X, an Ultra High Speed HDMI cable that supports HDMI 2.1 and an HDMI 2.1 TV, and says Series S owners who wish to game in 4K@120Hz need a certified Ultra High Speed HDMI cable; 'How to change the TV display settings' says 120Hz is only available for 1080p and 1440p. The ASUS and Lenovo spec pages we checked list the USB-C ports and DisplayPort support but no maximum external resolution or refresh rate. We do not guess it.
